canonical_topic: Local Fragmentation and Volatility of Electricity Spot Markets
definition: Electricity spot markets are inherently local: because power must be delivered the instant it is demanded and cannot be substituted from a different geographic location without pre-arranged transmission, the market fractures into many separate local spot markets, each with its own rules and its own supply/demand balance.
core_idea: Because actual demand isn't known in advance and supply has to be arranged ahead of time, an unexpected shift in local demand easily produces a shortage or glut, making local spot prices highly volatile and largely disconnected from neighboring markets.
key_points: Consumers can draw power on demand at any time; the utility must meet it instantly with no ability to substitute power sourced elsewhere.
Because supply commitments must be arranged in advance, an unexpected demand swing can create a local shortage or surplus.
Each local spot market sets its own price from local supply and demand, so spot prices can be extremely volatile.

A price spike in one region (e.g., an unplanned plant outage forcing expensive backup generation) does not necessarily spread to a nearby region if real-time power transfer between the two is not possible — the two markets can move independently.
relationships: Contrasts with forward-market pricing, which is driven by macroeconomics rather than short-term local imbalances
Related to regulated vs. deregulated market structure
trading_implications: Traders cannot assume price moves in one power market imply similar moves in an adjacent market; correlation across regions depends on whether real-time transfer capacity exists between them.
caveats: It is tempting to assume nearby markets move together the way liquid, transportable commodities do; for electricity this is often false because it cannot be moved/stored freely.
